cardiac-cycle.name: The cardiac cycle
cardiac-cycle.summary: One heartbeat is a sequence of filling and ejection: diastole, when the ventricles relax and fill, and systole, when they contract and pump.
body: Each cycle lasts about 0.8 seconds at rest. During diastole the mitral and tricuspid valves are open and blood flows passively from the atria into the ventricles; the atria then contract to add the final fifth. Ventricular systole begins as pressure rises, the mitral and tricuspid valves snap shut (the first heart sound, 'lub'), and once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure the aortic and pulmonary valves open and blood is ejected.

As the ventricles relax, pressure falls, the aortic and pulmonary valves close (the second heart sound, 'dub') and the cycle repeats. The valves make flow one-way; the papillary muscles and chordae tendineae stop the mitral and tricuspid leaflets bulging back into the atria.
The fraction of the end-diastolic volume that is ejected, the ejection fraction, is normally 55 to 70% and is the everyday measure of how well the left ventricle pumps.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Cardiac cycle
British Heart Foundation: How a healthy heart works

heart-rate.name: Heart rate
heart-rate.summary: How often the heart beats, set by the sinoatrial node and adjusted second by second by the autonomic nervous system and hormones.
body: The sinoatrial node in the wall of the right atrium fires spontaneously about 100 times a minute if left alone. At rest the vagus nerve slows it to a typical 60 to 100 beats per minute; sympathetic nerves and adrenaline speed it up during exercise, fear or fever.

Trained athletes often have resting rates in the 40s because each beat pumps more blood. Rates persistently above 100 (tachycardia) or below 60 (bradycardia) are only abnormal in context: a rate of 45 in a marathon runner is normal, in a fainting older adult it may signal heart block.
Heart rate is one of the vital signs and is measured at the radial pulse, on an ECG, or by pulse oximeters and wearables.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Cardiac physiology
NHS: How to check your pulse

blood-pressure.name: Blood pressure
blood-pressure.summary: The pressure blood exerts on artery walls: systolic at the peak of ejection, diastolic between beats.
body: Blood pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps each minute (cardiac output) and how hard it is to push that blood through the small arteries (peripheral resistance). The elastic aorta smooths the pulse; the muscular arterioles set resistance and are the main site of control.

Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch report pressure to the brainstem, which adjusts heart rate and vessel tone within seconds. Over hours and days the kidneys take over, adjusting salt and water excretion through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

Blood pressure is written as systolic over diastolic in millimetres of mercury. Values around 120/80 mmHg are typical; sustained readings of 140/90 mmHg or more define hypertension in most guidelines.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Blood flow, blood pressure and resistance
NHS: High blood pressure (hypertension)

cardiac-output.name: Cardiac output
cardiac-output.summary: The volume of blood the heart pumps per minute: heart rate multiplied by stroke volume, about five litres at rest.
body: Stroke volume, the amount ejected per beat, rises when the ventricle fills more (the Frank-Starling mechanism: a more stretched muscle contracts harder), when contractility increases under sympathetic drive, and when the resistance it pumps against falls.

During hard exercise cardiac output can reach 20 to 25 litres per minute in a fit adult, mostly through a faster rate and a larger stroke volume, while blood is redirected from the gut and kidneys to the muscles.
A failing heart cannot raise its output to meet demand; the resulting breathlessness on exertion and fluid retention are the hallmarks of heart failure.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Cardiac physiology
NHLBI: How the heart works

cardiac-conduction.name: Electrical conduction of the heart
cardiac-conduction.summary: A wiring system of specialised muscle cells spreads each heartbeat from the sinoatrial node through the atria, the atrioventricular node and the bundle branches to the ventricles.
body: The impulse starts in the sinoatrial node, sweeps across both atria (the P wave of the ECG) and reaches the atrioventricular node, which delays it for about a tenth of a second so the atria finish emptying. It then races down the bundle of His and the right and left bundle branches to the Purkinje fibres, depolarising the ventricles from the apex upward (the QRS complex). Recovery of the ventricles produces the T wave.

Because the wave follows a fixed path, its timing on an ECG reveals blocks (a long PR interval or a bundle branch block), extra pathways and the chaotic atrial activity of atrial fibrillation. Damaged muscle after a heart attack changes the shape of the QRS and ST segments.
Pacemakers replace a failing sinoatrial node or a blocked atrioventricular node; ablation destroys tissue that generates abnormal rhythms.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Cardiac muscle and electrical activity
NHS: Electrocardiogram (ECG)

circulation.name: Circulation
circulation.summary: Two circuits in series: the pulmonary circulation loads blood with oxygen in the lungs, the systemic circulation delivers it to every organ.
body: The right heart pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary arteries into the lungs, where it picks up oxygen and unloads carbon dioxide before returning through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium. The left heart pumps it into the aorta and on through arteries, arterioles and capillaries, where exchange with the tissues happens, then back through venules and veins to the right atrium.

Pressure falls along the way: from about 120 mmHg in the aorta to a few mmHg in the great veins. Veins hold about two thirds of the blood volume at any moment and return it to the heart with the help of valves, the muscle pump of the legs and the suction of breathing.
Special circuits exist: the hepatic portal system carries gut blood through the liver first, and the coronary circulation supplies the heart muscle itself during diastole.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Circulatory pathways
NHLBI: How the heart works

breathing.name: Breathing (ventilation)
breathing.summary: Air moves in and out because muscles change the volume of the chest: the diaphragm and external intercostals enlarge it for inspiration; relaxation and elastic recoil empty it.
body: When the diaphragm contracts its dome flattens and the ribs swing up and out, lowering pressure inside the chest below atmospheric pressure so air flows in. Quiet expiration is passive: the stretched lungs and chest wall recoil. Forced breathing recruits the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals to push air out, and the scalenes and sternocleidomastoids to pull the ribs up.

The rhythm is generated in the medulla and pons and adjusted by chemoreceptors that sense carbon dioxide and, to a lesser extent, oxygen. A rising carbon dioxide level is the strongest normal drive to breathe.
Airway resistance matters: narrowing the bronchi even slightly, as in asthma, greatly increases the work of breathing because resistance rises with the fourth power of the reduction in radius.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: The process of breathing
NHLBI: How the lungs work

gas-exchange.name: Gas exchange
gas-exchange.summary: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the thin wall between alveoli and capillaries by diffusion, driven by differences in partial pressure.
body: The lungs contain about 300 million alveoli with a combined surface close to the size of a tennis court, separated from blood by a membrane under a micrometre thick. Oxygen diffuses into the blood because its partial pressure in alveolar air (about 100 mmHg) exceeds that in returning venous blood (about 40 mmHg); carbon dioxide moves the other way down a smaller gradient because it diffuses twenty times more readily.

Efficient exchange needs ventilation and blood flow to be matched. Blood sent to unventilated alveoli (as in pneumonia) is not oxygenated, and ventilated alveoli without blood flow (as in pulmonary embolism) are wasted breath. The lungs partly correct this by constricting vessels in poorly ventilated regions.
Thickening of the membrane (fibrosis) or fluid in the alveoli (pulmonary oedema) slows diffusion, and oxygen, with its lower solubility, is affected first.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Gas exchange
NHLBI: How the lungs work

oxygen-transport.name: Oxygen transport
oxygen-transport.summary: Almost all oxygen travels bound to haemoglobin in red cells; how tightly it binds changes with the tissue's needs.
body: Each haemoglobin molecule carries four oxygen molecules, and a litre of arterial blood holds about 200 ml of oxygen, over 98% of it bound. The binding curve is S-shaped: haemoglobin loads fully in the lungs yet releases oxygen readily where partial pressure is low. Acid, heat and carbon dioxide, all produced by working tissue, shift the curve to release more (the Bohr effect).

Pulse oximeters estimate the percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen; 95 to 100% is normal at sea level. Anaemia lowers the amount of haemoglobin, so total oxygen delivery falls even when saturation reads normal, which is why a saturation reading alone can mislead.
Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 240 times more tightly than oxygen, and standard oximeters cannot tell the difference.

keyFacts.label: Oxygen per litre of arterial blood

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Transport of gases
NHS England: Pulse oximetry

co2-removal.name: Carbon dioxide removal and acid-base balance
co2-removal.summary: Carbon dioxide, the waste of metabolism, is carried mostly as bicarbonate and breathed out; the balance between the two sets blood acidity.
body: Tissues make about 200 ml of carbon dioxide a minute at rest. In the blood most of it reacts with water inside red cells to form bicarbonate and hydrogen ions; some binds to haemoglobin and a little dissolves. In the lungs the reaction reverses and the gas is exhaled.

Because carbon dioxide is an acid in solution, breathing controls blood pH within minutes: breathing faster lowers carbon dioxide and raises pH (respiratory alkalosis, as in panic-driven hyperventilation), breathing less does the opposite. The kidneys adjust bicarbonate over hours to days, giving a second, slower control.

Normal arterial pH is tightly held at 7.35 to 7.45. Diseases that trap air (COPD), drugs that suppress breathing (opioids) or metabolic crises (diabetic ketoacidosis) disturb this balance and are diagnosed with an arterial blood gas.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Transport of gases
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Acid-base balance

lung-volumes.name: Lung volumes and capacities
lung-volumes.summary: The amounts of air the lungs move and hold, measured by spirometry and used to separate obstructive from restrictive disease.
body: A quiet breath moves about half a litre (tidal volume). Above it lies the inspiratory reserve and below it the expiratory reserve; together with tidal volume these make the vital capacity, roughly 4 to 5 litres in an adult man. Even after the deepest expiration about 1.2 litres remains as residual volume, keeping the alveoli open.

Spirometry records the forced vital capacity (FVC) and the volume blown out in the first second (FEV1). Obstructive disease (asthma, COPD) narrows the airways so FEV1 falls out of proportion to FVC and the FEV1/FVC ratio drops below about 0.7. Restrictive disease (fibrosis, chest wall problems) shrinks all volumes but keeps the ratio normal.
Volumes fall with age, height and smoking and rise with training; reference values are matched to age, sex, height and ethnicity.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: The process of breathing
NHS: Spirometry

neurons.name: Neurons
neurons.summary: The nerve cell: a body with branching dendrites that receive signals and a single axon that carries them onward, sometimes for a metre.
body: The brain holds about 86 billion neurons, each connected to thousands of others through synapses. Dendrites collect incoming signals; if their sum crosses a threshold at the axon hillock, the neuron fires an all-or-nothing action potential down its axon. Axons are wrapped in myelin, a fatty insulation that lets the impulse jump between gaps and travel up to 120 metres per second.

Neurons communicate chemically: an arriving impulse releases a neurotransmitter such as glutamate, GABA, dopamine or acetylcholine into the synaptic gap, and the receiving cell is excited or inhibited depending on its receptors. Most drugs acting on the nervous system change this step.
Glial cells outnumber neurons and feed, insulate and protect them. Unlike most cells, adult neurons rarely divide, which is why injury to the brain and spinal cord is so hard to repair.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Nervous tissue
NINDS: Brain basics, know your brain

nerve-signals.name: Nerve signals
nerve-signals.summary: Information travels as brief electrical pulses, action potentials, whose rate carries the message; at synapses it becomes chemical.
body: An action potential is a wave of sodium ions rushing into the axon followed by potassium flowing out, restoring the resting state within a millisecond. Because each pulse is identical, a stronger stimulus is signalled by more pulses per second, not bigger ones.

Sensory signals travel from receptors through the spinal cord and thalamus to the cortex; motor commands travel down the corticospinal tract, cross to the opposite side in the medulla, and leave through spinal nerves. This crossing is why a stroke in the left hemisphere weakens the right side of the body.

Local anaesthetics block sodium channels so pain signals never start; multiple sclerosis strips myelin so signals slow or fail; nerve compression, as in carpal tunnel syndrome, produces tingling and numbness along the nerve's territory.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: The action potential
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Communication between neurons

reflexes.name: Reflexes
reflexes.summary: Fast, automatic responses wired through the spinal cord or brainstem that protect the body before the brain has time to decide.
body: The knee-jerk is the simplest: tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps, a sensory neuron fires straight onto a motor neuron in the spinal cord, and the muscle contracts. Withdrawal from a hot object uses one more neuron and also inhibits the opposing muscles. Brainstem reflexes include the pupil's response to light, the gag and cough reflexes and the baroreceptor reflex that steadies blood pressure.

Clinicians grade tendon reflexes because they map the nervous system: a lost ankle reflex points to the S1 nerve root, brisk reflexes with a spreading pattern point to damage above the spinal cord, as after a stroke.
Reflexes can be modulated: the brain can suppress a withdrawal to keep hold of a hot cup, and spinal cord injury releases reflexes from that control, producing spasticity.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Motor responses
NINDS: Brain basics, know your brain

brain-functions.name: Brain functions
brain-functions.summary: Different regions specialise: the cortex for perception, movement, language and thought; deep nuclei for movement and emotion; the brainstem for life support; the cerebellum for coordination.
body: The frontal lobe plans, decides and, through the precentral gyrus, commands movement; Broca's area in the left inferior frontal gyrus produces speech. The parietal lobe handles touch and space, the temporal lobe hearing, memory and language comprehension (Wernicke's area), and the occipital lobe vision. The insula senses the body's internal state.

Beneath the cortex, the basal ganglia select and smooth movements, the thalamus relays almost every signal to the cortex, the hypothalamus runs hormones, temperature, hunger and sleep, and the hippocampus lays down new memories. The brainstem keeps breathing and the heart going and houses the cranial nerve nuclei; the cerebellum times and coordinates movement.

Because functions are localised, the pattern of a deficit locates a lesion: right-sided weakness with lost speech points to the left middle cerebral artery territory, unsteadiness to the cerebellum, and memory loss with preserved alertness to the medial temporal lobes.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: The central nervous system
NINDS: Brain basics, know your brain

sensory-systems.name: Sensory systems
sensory-systems.summary: Receptors convert light, sound, chemicals, pressure and temperature into nerve signals that the thalamus and cortex turn into perception.
body: The eye focuses light onto the retina, where rods handle dim light and cones colour; signals cross partly at the optic chiasm so each visual cortex sees the opposite half of the world. The ear turns vibration into fluid waves in the cochlea, where hair cells fire in proportion to pitch; the neighbouring semicircular canals and otolith organs sense rotation and gravity for balance.

Smell receptors in the roof of the nose project directly to the olfactory cortex and limbic system, which is why odours evoke memory so strongly; taste buds detect sweet, salt, sour, bitter and umami. Skin carries receptors for touch, vibration, temperature and pain, with the fingertips and lips most densely supplied and therefore over-represented in the sensory cortex.
Pain is a protective signal, not a measurement of damage: it is amplified by inflammation and modulated by the brain, which explains phantom limb pain and the relief of distraction.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Sensory perception
NHS: Hearing loss

digestion.name: Digestion
digestion.summary: Food is broken down mechanically by chewing and churning and chemically by enzymes, from starch in the mouth to proteins and fats in the small intestine.
body: Chewing mixes food with saliva, whose amylase starts on starch. The stomach adds hydrochloric acid, which unfolds proteins and kills microbes, and pepsin, which begins their breakdown; it churns the mix into a paste called chyme and releases it into the duodenum a few millilitres at a time.

In the duodenum, bile from the liver emulsifies fat into droplets and pancreatic juice supplies the main enzymes: lipase for fat, amylase for starch and proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin) for protein. Enzymes on the intestinal lining finish the job, splitting sugars and peptides into single molecules ready for absorption.

Digestion is regulated by nerves and hormones: the sight and smell of food prime the stomach (vagus nerve), gastrin drives acid, and cholecystokinin from the duodenum squeezes the gallbladder and slows the stomach when fat arrives.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Digestive system processes and regulation
NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works

absorption.name: Absorption
absorption.summary: Nutrients cross the lining of the small intestine into blood and lymph; the colon reclaims water and salts.
body: The small intestine's folds, finger-like villi and microscopic microvilli multiply its surface area to around 30 square metres. Sugars and amino acids are pumped into the cells and pass into capillaries that drain to the portal vein and the liver. Fats are rebuilt inside the cells into chylomicrons and enter the lymphatic lacteals, bypassing the liver at first.

Iron and calcium are absorbed mainly in the duodenum, most other nutrients in the jejunum, and vitamin B12 and bile salts only in the terminal ileum, which is why disease or surgery there causes specific deficiencies.

About nine litres of fluid enter the gut daily (drink plus secretions); the small intestine absorbs most and the colon nearly all the rest, leaving about 100 ml in stool. Diarrhoea is a failure of this reclamation.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Chemical digestion and absorption
NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works

gut-motility.name: Gut motility
gut-motility.summary: Coordinated waves of smooth muscle contraction (peristalsis) move contents along the tract, run by the gut's own nervous system and tuned by the vagus nerve and hormones.
body: Swallowing is voluntary at the start, then reflex: the oesophagus carries a bolus to the stomach in about ten seconds, and the lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes to let it through and then closes to keep acid out. The stomach mixes with slow waves three times a minute; the small intestine segments to mix and propels to move; between meals a housekeeping wave sweeps residue toward the colon every 90 minutes or so.

The colon moves contents slowly, with a few strong mass movements a day, often after meals, that push stool into the rectum and trigger the urge to defecate. The internal anal sphincter relaxes automatically; the external sphincter and puborectalis are under voluntary control.
Motility disorders cause reflux, gastroparesis, constipation or irritable bowel symptoms; a mechanical block (obstruction) produces cramping pain, vomiting and absence of gas.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Digestive system processes and regulation
NIDDK: Your digestive system and how it works

liver-functions.name: Liver functions
liver-functions.summary: The liver processes everything absorbed from the gut, stores and releases fuel, makes most blood proteins, detoxifies drugs and produces bile.
body: Portal blood arrives loaded with nutrients and anything else absorbed. Liver cells store glucose as glycogen and release it between meals, make new glucose from amino acids when needed, build and break down fats and cholesterol, and manufacture albumin and the clotting factors. Ammonia from protein breakdown is converted to urea for the kidneys to excrete.

Enzyme systems (the cytochrome P450 family) transform drugs, alcohol and toxins into water-soluble forms for excretion; this is why liver disease changes drug doses and why paracetamol overdose is so dangerous. Old red cells are broken down and their haem becomes bilirubin, which the liver conjugates and excretes in bile; when this fails, bilirubin accumulates and the skin turns yellow (jaundice).
Bile, about half a litre a day, is stored in the gallbladder and released to emulsify dietary fat. The liver can regenerate after losing more than half its mass.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Accessory organs in digestion
NIDDK: Liver disease

pancreatic-functions.name: Pancreatic functions
pancreatic-functions.summary: One organ, two jobs: exocrine cells pour digestive enzymes and bicarbonate into the duodenum; the islets of Langerhans release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
body: About 1.5 litres of alkaline pancreatic juice a day neutralises stomach acid and delivers lipase, amylase and the protein-digesting enzymes, which are secreted as inactive precursors and switched on only in the gut so the pancreas does not digest itself. When that safeguard fails, the result is pancreatitis.

The islets sense blood glucose directly. After a meal beta cells release insulin, which tells muscle, fat and liver to take up and store glucose; between meals alpha cells release glucagon, which makes the liver release it again. This pair holds blood glucose within a narrow band around 4 to 7 mmol/L.
Type 1 diabetes destroys the beta cells; type 2 diabetes is mainly resistance to insulin's signal with a gradual failure of the beta cells to compensate.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Accessory organs in digestion
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: The endocrine pancreas

filtration.name: Glomerular filtration
filtration.summary: Blood pressure forces water and small solutes out of the glomerular capillaries into the nephron, about 180 litres a day, while cells and proteins stay behind.
body: Each kidney holds about a million nephrons. In the glomerulus a tuft of leaky capillaries sits inside Bowman's capsule; the pressure difference drives an ultrafiltrate of plasma through a three-layer sieve that blocks cells and almost all protein. The glomerular filtration rate (GFR), roughly 120 ml per minute in a healthy young adult, is the standard measure of kidney function.

The kidney keeps GFR steady across a wide range of blood pressures by adjusting its afferent and efferent arterioles; drugs that act on these vessels (NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors) can drop filtration in a dehydrated patient.
Because creatinine is filtered freely and barely reabsorbed, its blood level rises as GFR falls, which is how kidney disease is staged. Protein in the urine means the sieve is damaged.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Physiology of urine formation
NIDDK: Your kidneys and how they work

reabsorption.name: Tubular reabsorption and secretion
reabsorption.summary: The tubules reclaim over 99% of the filtered water and salt and all the glucose, and add wastes and excess ions to what remains.
body: The proximal tubule recovers about two thirds of the filtered water and sodium and all the glucose and amino acids; when blood glucose is high, as in uncontrolled diabetes, the transporters are overwhelmed and glucose spills into the urine. The loop of Henle builds a salt gradient in the medulla that allows water to be drawn out later. The distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune sodium, potassium and acid under hormonal control.

Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption (and potassium loss); antidiuretic hormone opens water channels in the collecting duct to concentrate urine. Diuretic drugs block specific transporters: loop diuretics in the thick ascending limb, thiazides in the distal tubule.
Secretion works the other way: the tubules actively pump potassium, hydrogen ions, drugs and organic acids into the urine, which is how penicillin and many other drugs are cleared.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Tubular reabsorption
NIDDK: Your kidneys and how they work

urine-formation.name: Urine formation and excretion
urine-formation.summary: Filtration, reabsorption and secretion leave one to two litres of urine a day, carried by the ureters to the bladder and released under voluntary control.
body: Urine is mostly water carrying urea, creatinine, uric acid, salts and any drug metabolites the body needs to lose. Its colour reflects concentration; its composition, read by a dipstick, reveals infection (leucocytes, nitrites), blood, protein, glucose or ketones.

Peristalsis in the ureters delivers urine to the bladder, which stretches to hold 400 to 600 ml. Stretch receptors signal fullness at around 200 ml; the micturition reflex contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter, while the external sphincter is released voluntarily. Children learn this control between two and four years; strokes, spinal injury and prostate enlargement disturb it.
Kidney stones form when salts crystallise in concentrated urine; keeping urine dilute is the simplest prevention.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Physiology of urine formation
NIDDK: Your kidneys and how they work

fluid-balance.name: Fluid balance
fluid-balance.summary: Water in equals water out: thirst, antidiuretic hormone and the kidneys keep the body's 40 litres of fluid within a litre of its set point.
body: An adult is about 60% water: two thirds inside cells, the rest in the tissue spaces and in blood plasma. Intake of about 2.5 litres a day (drink, food and metabolism) matches loss in urine, sweat, breath and stool. Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense a rise in blood concentration of only 1 to 2% and trigger both thirst and antidiuretic hormone, which makes the kidneys retain water.

Volume is sensed separately by stretch receptors in the heart and pressure receptors in the arteries; a fall activates the sympathetic system and the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone cascade, which retains salt and water and constricts vessels. Heart failure and cirrhosis activate these pathways inappropriately and cause swelling (oedema).
Dehydration presents with thirst, dark urine, dizziness on standing and a rising heart rate; in infants and the elderly it can progress quickly.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Body fluids and fluid compartments
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Water balance

electrolytes.name: Electrolytes
electrolytes.summary: Sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride and bicarbonate carry charge, set the water distribution between compartments and make nerves and muscles excitable.
body: Sodium is the main ion outside cells and, with its water, sets blood volume; the kidneys and aldosterone keep its concentration near 140 mmol/L. Potassium is concentrated inside cells; its blood level, normally 3.5 to 5, must stay in a narrow band because both high and low values disturb the heart's rhythm.

Calcium is regulated by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D and is needed for muscle contraction, clotting and nerve signalling; low levels cause tingling and cramps, high levels stones, bone pain and confusion. Magnesium is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and follows potassium.
Vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretics, kidney disease and hormone disorders are the usual causes of imbalance, detected on a basic metabolic panel.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Electrolyte balance
NHS: Blood tests

hormones.name: Hormones
hormones.summary: Chemical messengers released into the blood that act on distant cells carrying the right receptor, coordinating growth, metabolism, stress and reproduction over minutes to years.
body: Hormones come in families. Peptides and proteins (insulin, growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone) act on surface receptors and work within minutes. Steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, oestrogen) are made from cholesterol, pass into cells and switch genes on or off over hours. Amines include adrenaline, fast and short-lived, and thyroid hormone, slow and long-lasting.

The same hormone can do different things in different tissues: adrenaline speeds the heart, dilates airways and releases glucose all at once, which is exactly what a fight-or-flight response needs. Concentrations are tiny, measured in picomoles, so small changes matter and assays must be precise.
Because hormones reach everywhere, endocrine disease is multi-system: an overactive thyroid causes weight loss, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance and anxiety together.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Hormones
Society for Endocrinology: You and your hormones

hormone-regulation.name: Hormone regulation: the hypothalamic-pituitary axis
hormone-regulation.summary: The hypothalamus tells the pituitary, the pituitary tells the glands, and the glands' hormones report back: a chain of command that links the brain to the endocrine system.
body: Releasing hormones from the hypothalamus travel down a private portal system to the anterior pituitary, which secretes the tropic hormones: thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, the gonadotropins, growth hormone and prolactin. The posterior pituitary stores two hormones made in the hypothalamus itself, antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin.

Each axis is a loop: for the thyroid, TRH drives TSH, TSH drives thyroxine, and thyroxine suppresses both. So a failing thyroid produces a high TSH, while a pituitary problem produces low TSH with low thyroxine; the pair of results tells you where the fault lies.
Stress, sleep, light and season act on the hypothalamus, which is why cortisol peaks in the early morning, growth hormone surges in deep sleep and the menstrual cycle can stop under severe stress.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: The pituitary gland and hypothalamus
Society for Endocrinology: Pituitary gland

feedback-mechanisms.name: Feedback mechanisms and homeostasis
feedback-mechanisms.summary: Negative feedback, where a rise in the output switches off its own production, holds temperature, glucose, blood pressure and hormones near their set points.
body: A thermostat is the model: a sensor measures the variable, a control centre compares it with a set point, and an effector corrects the error. Body temperature is held near 37 °C by the hypothalamus, which orders sweating and skin vasodilation when hot and shivering and vasoconstriction when cold; fever is a deliberate resetting of the set point by inflammatory signals.

Glucose is held by the insulin-glucagon pair, calcium by parathyroid hormone, blood pressure by baroreflexes and the kidneys, oxygen and carbon dioxide by the breathing centres. Diseases are often a broken loop: in type 1 diabetes the effector (insulin) is missing; in Cushing's disease the control centre ignores the feedback.
Positive feedback is rare and used for events that must run to completion: the surge of oxytocin in labour, blood clotting and the sodium rush of an action potential.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Homeostasis
OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: Hormones

endocrine-glands.name: The major endocrine glands
endocrine-glands.summary: Pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals, pancreatic islets, gonads and pineal each make a signature set of hormones; several other organs, including the heart, kidneys, gut and fat, make hormones too.
body: The pituitary controls growth, thyroid and adrenal function, reproduction, milk production and water balance. The thyroid sets the metabolic rate through thyroxine; the four parathyroids behind it raise blood calcium. The adrenal cortex makes cortisol (stress and glucose), aldosterone (salt and blood pressure) and androgens; its medulla makes adrenaline. The islets of the pancreas make insulin and glucagon; the testes make testosterone and the ovaries oestrogen and progesterone; the pineal makes melatonin.

Less famous sources matter clinically: the heart releases natriuretic peptides when stretched (used to diagnose heart failure), the kidneys release erythropoietin to make red cells, the gut makes incretins that boost insulin, and fat tissue makes leptin, which signals energy stores to the brain.
In this atlas the pituitary and adrenal glands are modelled; the thyroid and parathyroids are not part of the dataset.

references.title: OpenStax Anatomy & Physiology 2e: An overview of the endocrine system
Society for Endocrinology: Glands
